successors.note: 'Starting in 1114, Aguda united the Jurchen tribes under his rule and rebelled against the Liao dynasty'; 'In January 1115 ... proclaimed himself emperor, established the Jin' (Wanyan Aguda page); infobox 'Founded by Aguda: 28 January 1115' (Jin page); the Timeline page has 'spring' 1115. The great-jin dossier names this slug as predecessor.

rulers.name: Wanyan Helibo
rulers.note: '1074: Wugunai of the Wanyan clan unites the Jurchens of eastern and northern Manchuria' and is succeeded by his son Helibo.

rulers.name: Wanyan Wuyashu
rulers.note: Succeeded his uncle in 1103 ('Yingge is succeeded by his nephew Wanyan Wuyashu'); the Jurchen page says Goryeo-Jurchen relations 'began to change' under him (r. 1103-1113), and the Wanyan took Chongju in 1104.

rulers.name: Wanyan Aguda
rulers.note: Succeeded his brother Wuyashu in 1113 (born 1068 near the Ashi river, Wanyan Aguda page); declared the Jin in 1115.

correction.text: eastern and northern Manchuria outside the Liao's land: the Jurchen country of Heilongjiang and Jilin

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe for a state Cliopatria lacks: no Cliopatria shape covers Heilongjiang and Jilin outside the Liao's land in 1074-1114 (its Liao shape of 1040 takes 263 thousand km2 of the two provinces). '1074: Wugunai of the Wanyan clan unites the Jurchens of eastern and northern Manchuria'; the Jurchen page: 'There is no dated evidence of the Jurchens before the time of Wugunai (1021-74)' and the Jurchens 'began to coalesce into a nation-like federation'. The Jurchens first appear in Chinese records in 748 'in the forests and river valleys' of Heilongjiang and Primorsky Krai, and had become Liao vassals 'by the 11th century'. No page gives an area or boundary; the shape is the Manchuria region minus Cliopatria's Liao shape of 1040 (546 thousand km2, 121.3-134.6 E, 44.3-53.6 N; confidence 1). Primorsky Krai is left out (the pages mention it only in the 748 description of the Jurchens' forests).

region.text: eastern and northern Manchuria outside the Liao's land: the Jurchen country of Heilongjiang and Jilin

ledger.note: 1074: Wugunai unites the Jurchens. 'Wugunai of the Wanyan clan unites the Jurchens of eastern and northern Manchuria' and is succeeded by his son Wanyan Helibo (Timeline page); the Jurchen page puts no dated evidence of the Jurchens before Wugunai (1021-74). The shape is the researcher's reading of 'eastern and northern Manchuria' (confidence 2). The pages give no earlier federation: the Jurchens appear in 748 as tribute-bearers to the Tang, bore tribute to the Later Tang in 925 and the Song in 961, raided the Liao in 973 and 976.

1104: 'The Wanyan clan enters Goryeo territory in pursuit of enemy tribes, defeats Im Gan, and takes Chongju castle' (Timeline page); the Jurchen page: 'In 1104, the Wanyan Jurchens reached Chongju'. The Goryeo dossier records the same zone as Hamgyong-namdo; it calls the counterpart 'jurchens'.

region.text: the Nine Fortresses, traditionally at Hamhung

ledger.note: December 1107: 'A Goryeo invasion led by Yun Kwan enters Jurchen territory and builds the Nine Fortresses in the area' (Timeline page); 'In December 1107, Yun Kwan and O Yonch'on set out with 170,000 soldiers' (Jurchen page). The goryeo dossier records the matching gain with the counterpart 'jurchens'. The Nine Fortresses are not placed on either page; Hamgyong-namdo follows the goryeo dossier.

region.text: the Nine Fortresses, traditionally at Hamhung

ledger.note: 1108: 'Goryeo returns the Nine Fortresses region to the Wanyan clan, possibly in exchange for Poju (Uiju), and Yun Kwan is removed from office' (Timeline page); the goryeo dossier records the matching loss.
1108: the Goryeo-Jurchen fighting ends with the return of the Nine Fortresses (the goryeo dossier runs the war to 1109 on its infobox).

region.text: Ningjiangzhou, Huanglong and the Jin heartland

ledger.note: November 1114: the Jurchens take Ningjiangzhou and win at Chuhedian. He 'captured Ningjiangzhou' and beat 7,000 Liao there (Wanyan Aguda page; the liao-dynasty dossier records the same zone with the counterpart great-jin).

region.text: Ningjiangzhou, Huanglong and the Jin heartland

ledger.note: January 1115: the Jin is proclaimed; the war with the Liao passes to the great-jin dossier. In August Aguda conquered Huanglong Prefecture.

wars.name: Jurchen-Goryeo war
wars.outcome: 1104: the Wanyan clan took Chongju and beat Im Gan; December 1107: Yun Kwan's 170,000 men built the Nine Fortresses; 1108: Goryeo returned the Nine Fortresses region to the Wanyan clan.
wars.note: The Goryeo dossier dates the war 1104-1109 (infobox) and calls the counterpart 'jurchens'.

wars.name: Jurchen revolt against the Liao

zones.text: Ningjiangzhou, Huanglong and the Jin heartland

wars.outcome: September 1114 Aguda rallied 2,500 men at Liushui and rebelled; November 1114 he took Ningjiangzhou and beat 7,000 Liao at Chuhedian; January 1115 he proclaimed the Jin.
wars.note: The liao-dynasty dossier carries the whole conflict to 1125 under great-jin.

notes:
State Cliopatria lacks: no Cliopatria shape covers the Jurchen country (Cliopatria's Liao row stops at Heilongjiang's south-west; its Jin row starts in 1126). The great-jin dossier already names this slug as predecessor and carries 1115 onward.

Dated by the pages: the federation starts with Wugunai (1021-74), 'There is no dated evidence of the Jurchens before the time of Wugunai'; 748 is the first mention of the Jurchens; 1104-1108 the Goryeo war; 1113 Aguda succeeds; 1114-1115 the revolt. The pages give no area, no boundary and no earlier federation; the Jurchen tribes before 1074 (748: Heilongjiang and Primorsky Krai) are not drawn. Tribute missions (925 Later Tang, 961 Song), raids on the Liao (973, 976) and the Goryeo forts of 994-996 and attacks of 1051, 1056 and 1080 are tribal events before or outside the confederation's dates and are not in the ledger.

Naming. The goryeo dossier calls this state 'jurchens' in its events of 1104, 1107 and 1108; the liao-dynasty dossier names the counterpart great-jin for the 1114-1125 war. The Hamgyong-namdo strip (Chongju, the Nine Fortresses) is drawn for 1104-1106 and 1108-1114 only; the Timeline page puts the return of the Nine Fortresses region to the Wanyan clan in 1108 ('possibly in exchange for Poju'). The Liao suzerainty ('By the 11th century, the Jurchens had become vassals of the Khitan rulers of the Liao dynasty', no year; ended by Aguda's rebellion in September 1114) is recorded as a vassal pair in the liao-dynasty dossier, with this slug as counterpart.
